sections.title: An organ, a cell and a signal
paragraphs: An ovary, an egg and estrogen all belong in an explanation of reproduction. But they do different jobs. If we treat the three names as interchangeable, we lose the connection between the structure that produces something and the product that leaves it.

A gonad is a reproductive organ that produces gametes and releases reproductive hormones. The testes are the male gonads, and the ovaries are the female gonads. A gamete is a reproductive cell: a sperm or an egg. A hormone is a chemical messenger. Testosterone, estrogen and progesterone are examples of reproductive hormones.

Consider a testis. Sperm develop in tiny tubes within the organ, while other cells release testosterone into the blood. The sperm can travel through reproductive ducts. Testosterone travels in the blood to tissues able to respond to it. One organ contributes both a cell and a signal, but those products have different routes and functions.

A human gamete normally carries one set of 23 chromosomes. At fertilization, a sperm and an egg contribute one set each, so the resulting cell has 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes. The gonad does not leave the parent and join another gonad. The cells it helps produce carry the chromosome contributions. The details of chromosome separation will come with meiosis.

sections.title: What makes a characteristic primary or secondary?
paragraphs: Primary sex characteristics are the reproductive organs and structures themselves. Testes, ovaries, reproductive ducts, the uterus, penis and vagina belong in this category. Most of these structures are present at birth and continue to develop. Primary names a biological category; it does not mean more important.

Secondary sex characteristics are other physical features associated with sexual maturation. Examples include facial-hair growth, a deeper voice and breast development. They become more noticeable as hormone activity changes during puberty. The examples describe patterns with considerable variation among people, rather than a checklist everyone must match.

Now compare an ovary becoming more active with breast development. Both can change during puberty. The ovary remains a reproductive organ, so it remains a primary characteristic. Breast development belongs to the secondary category used here. The timing is similar; the kind of structure or feature is different. That is why the observation 'it changed at puberty' cannot settle the classification by itself.

A reproductive duct is also primary even though it does not make gametes. An oviduct, for example, helps transport the egg toward the uterus. Primary characteristics include structures that support transport and other reproductive functions, not just the gonads.

sections.title: How a chromosome signal reaches a developing tissue
paragraphs: In the typical chromosome patterns considered here, XX is associated with female reproductive development and XY with male reproductive development. X and Y are called sex chromosomes. These chromosome combinations are established at fertilization, before the reproductive organs have taken their later form. The chromosome pattern and the developed anatomy describe different parts of the explanation.

A gene is a stretch of DNA containing information used by cells. SRY is a gene usually carried on the Y chromosome. Its activity helps initiate testis development. Hormones from the developing testes, including testosterone, then contribute to the development of reproductive tissues. The sequence links genetic information, an organ that develops, and signals produced by that organ. Testosterone alone does not explain every reproductive structure.

A hormone produces its usual effect only when a target cell can respond. A receptor is a molecule in or on a cell that recognises a particular signal. A hormone can be present in the blood while a tissue lacking a functioning receptor has a reduced or absent response to it. Measuring the signal therefore does not tell us everything about the tissue's response.

The XX/XY account is a model of typical development. Variations in genes, hormone production and tissue responses also occur. Use the stated model when explaining the biology, and keep conclusions within its information. These anatomy categories do not determine a person's identity.

sections.title: Puberty brings existing structures into new activity
paragraphs: Puberty is a period of increased reproductive hormone activity and developing reproductive capacity. The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, and the anterior pituitary, a hormone-releasing gland below it, help coordinate signals to the gonads. The reproductive organs develop further, gamete-related activity changes, and secondary characteristics become more apparent.

These changes connect the ideas we have separated. A gonad is the organ; a gamete is a reproductive cell; a hormone is a signal. A primary structure can become more active at puberty without changing category. A secondary feature is classified by what it is, rather than just when it appeared.

When you explain a new observation, name the structure or product first. Then follow its route and describe its effect. We will use that approach to follow sperm from their production site through the male reproductive ducts.

worked.title: A hormone is present, but one tissue responds differently
worked.scenario: In a stated classroom model, two tissues receive the same reproductive hormone from the blood. Tissue A has functioning receptors for it. Tissue B lacks functioning receptors for it. Other conditions needed for the response are the same. Does the shared hormone supply establish that both tissues respond normally?
steps: Identify what is shared: both tissues receive the chemical signal. This information concerns hormone delivery, not the production of gametes or the presence of a gonad.

Identify what differs: the tissues' receptors. A functioning receptor allows the target cell to recognise the signal. Tissue A can make the usual response under the stated conditions. Tissue B's response will be reduced or absent.

Check the proposed conclusion against both requirements. Delivery is present in both tissues, but the ability to respond is not. The same hormone supply is therefore insufficient to establish the same response.
Keep the conclusion bounded. This model changes a receptor condition. It does not tell us that Tissue B changed its chromosome number or that the hormone became a sperm or egg.

optional.question: A description names a uterus, an egg and progesterone. Which is a reproductive organ, which is a gamete, and which is a hormone? Is every reproductive organ a gonad? Explain the distinction before checking.
optional.answer: The uterus is a reproductive organ, the egg is a gamete and progesterone is a hormone. A gonad specifically produces gametes and reproductive hormones. The uterus supports development but is not an ovary or testis and does not produce gametes. The word reproductive therefore describes a wider group of organs than the word gonad.

sections.title: Locate production before tracing the journey
paragraphs: A sperm cell must be produced, mature and travel out of the body. Those jobs happen in connected structures. We will follow the connections rather than make a route out of every nearby label in an anatomy picture.

The two testes lie in the scrotum, a pouch outside the main body cavity. Sperm production works best a little below core body temperature. Moving the testes closer to the body in cold conditions helps retain heat; holding them farther away in warmer conditions helps lose heat. The scrotum helps provide suitable conditions for the organs inside it.

Within each testis, tightly coiled seminiferous tubules are the sperm-production sites. Sperm pass from them through small connecting ducts into the epididymis, a long coiled duct alongside the testis. In the epididymis, sperm mature, acquire the capacity for movement and can be stored. Production and maturation are connected stages at different locations.

Look at the lower part of the side-view diagram. The testis is the oval organ inside the scrotum. Follow the epididymis label to the curved structure along the testis, then find the ductus deferens leaving this region. The black lines connect names to structures; they are label lines, not arrows showing sperm movement. The picture shows a cut-away side view and does not display every small internal duct or the coiled seminiferous tubules.

sections.title: Follow the connected ducts
paragraphs: During ejaculation, coordinated muscular contractions move sperm from the epididymis into the vas deferens. Ductus deferens is another name for this same duct. It carries sperm upward from the testis region and into the pelvis.

At the next junction, the vas deferens joins the duct of a seminal vesicle. The resulting ejaculatory duct carries the mixture through the prostate into the urethra. The urethra then runs through the penis to the outside. The penis is the organ containing that final passage, rather than an extra sperm-producing site. During intercourse, it can deposit semen in the female reproductive tract.

Return to the figure. Trace the labelled ductus deferens upward and around the bladder region, then locate the short ejaculatory duct near the seminal vesicle and prostate. Find the urethra continuing through the penis. The path passes near the urinary bladder; it does not go through the bladder's storage space.

The male urethra is shared by the urinary and reproductive systems, but urine and semen are normally released at different times. The ureter is a different tube: it brings urine to the bladder. Similar names and neighbouring positions do not make the ureter part of the sperm pathway. For the main reproductive route, keep the sequence seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra.

sections.title: Why the travelling mixture is called semen
paragraphs: Sperm are cells. Semen is the mixture containing sperm and fluid from accessory glands. Accessory means that the glands contribute to the reproductive system without being the gonads that produce the sperm. A gland releases a secretion; a transport duct carries material along a passage.

The seminal vesicles add fructose-containing fluid. Fructose is a sugar that sperm can use as an energy source. The prostate contributes fluid to semen through ducts entering the urethral region. The bulbourethral glands, also called Cowper's glands, release lubricating mucus into the urethra. The combined secretions support sperm activity and help provide a suitable fluid environment, including buffering acidity. A buffer helps resist changes in acidity.

Use the diagram to separate the gland bodies from the route. The seminal vesicle lies behind the bladder, the prostate lies below it around the beginning of the urethra, and Cowper's gland is shown lower down. Secretions reach the route through gland ducts. A sperm does not have to travel through the interior of every gland to receive the fluid it adds.

A fluid sample and a cell sample tell us different things. Seeing fluid leave a gland would establish secretion, not sperm production. Finding sperm in the travelling mixture would identify cells that originated in seminiferous tubules. The name semen describes the combined material and does not make every component come from one structure.

sections.title: Keep the cell route and hormone route separate
paragraphs: The testes also contain interstitial cells, also called Leydig cells, between the seminiferous tubules. These cells release testosterone into the blood. This is an endocrine route: a hormone enters the circulation and reaches responsive tissues. Sperm instead travel through the reproductive duct system. The same organ contributes to both routes, but the routes are physically different.

A useful explanation follows the affected function. A change to a production site first concerns cell production. A change to an epididymis can affect maturation or storage. A change to a transport duct concerns passage along that route. A change in a gland's secretion concerns a fluid contribution. After identifying the first effect, trace which downstream parts depend on it and which still have their own functioning sources.

For an illustration with two testes and paired ducts, check whether a question describes one side or both before claiming that all sperm transport is interrupted. These classroom cases isolate a mechanism; they do not give enough information to diagnose a person's fertility.

We can now connect the journey to the starting question. Seminiferous tubules supply sperm, the epididymis supports maturation, ducts transport them, and accessory glands add fluid. Next, a closer view inside a testis will let us distinguish the cells that become sperm from the cells that support them.

worked.title: A changed gland secretion with an open sperm route
worked.scenario: In a simplified model, sperm production and maturation continue normally and all transport ducts remain open. Only the seminal vesicles' fructose contribution is reduced. What changes directly, and what cannot be concluded from that change alone?
steps: Locate the changed source. The seminal vesicles are accessory glands. They contribute fructose-containing fluid rather than producing the sperm cells.
Follow that contribution into the mixture. Less fructose from these glands reduces an energy-source contribution available to sperm in the seminal fluid. It may affect support for sperm activity.

Check the unchanged conditions. The problem explicitly keeps sperm production, maturation and duct transport functioning. It therefore does not establish that no sperm can enter the mixture or that the urethra is blocked.
Separate the other route as well. Testosterone enters blood from interstitial cells. A changed fructose contribution does not itself show that testosterone release stopped.

Conclude at the level the evidence supports: the gland contribution has changed. The model supplies no measurements that would let us calculate sperm speed, an exact sperm count or a probability of fertilization.

optional.question: In a second model, both testes still produce sperm but passage through both epididymides is completely interrupted. Accessory glands and their downstream ducts remain open. Explain which material loses its route and whether gland fluid must also disappear. Then identify one difference from the worked gland-secretion example.
optional.answer: Newly produced sperm cannot pass through the interrupted epididymides to reach the downstream sperm ducts. Accessory-gland fluid still has its own downstream entry points, so it need not disappear. This prediction concerns new transport after the interruption; it does not determine whether sperm were already stored farther along before it occurred. Unlike the worked example, this model changes a cell-transport route rather than only the composition of a gland secretion.

sections.title: Different cells share the same testis
paragraphs: A testis produces sperm and releases testosterone. That does not mean one kind of cell does both jobs. To explain sperm production, we need to look inside the organ and separate the developing reproductive cells from the cells that support and regulate them.

Spermatogenesis is the process of producing sperm in the seminiferous tubules, the tightly coiled tubes inside a testis. These developing reproductive cells are also called germ cells. They belong to a lineage in which successive stages lead toward sperm. More developed cells are generally closer to the lumen, the inner space of the tubule, where sperm are released.

A Sertoli cell lies within a seminiferous tubule and supports the developing cells. It supplies nourishment and helps maintain their local environment. It remains a supporting cell rather than becoming a sperm. Interstitial cells, also called Leydig cells, lie between the tubules and release testosterone. Inside a tubule and between tubules are different locations with different functions.

In the figure, begin at A with the organ and its coiled tubules. The enlarged view B shows sections through tubules; the interstitial-cell label points to tissue between them. In D, find the tall Sertoli cell beside the smaller developing cells, then follow the developing cells toward the sperm at the right. The broad curved arrows connect enlarged or related views; they do not mean that an interstitial cell turns into a Sertoli cell or a sperm. Panel C shows the specialised cell produced by the reproductive-cell lineage.

sections.title: Two divisions, followed by a change of form
paragraphs: The starting reproductive cells are called spermatogonia; one is a spermatogonium. They divide by mitosis, a cell-division process that maintains a supply of starting cells. Some descendants develop into primary spermatocytes. Before a primary spermatocyte begins meiosis, its DNA has been copied.

Meiosis is a process with two successive divisions. Meiosis I takes one primary spermatocyte to two secondary spermatocytes. Meiosis II divides each secondary spermatocyte, giving four spermatids in total. Count the cells at each step: one becomes two, then each of those two becomes two, so 2 × 2 = 4. There is no extra DNA-copying stage between meiosis I and meiosis II.

The four spermatids are haploid: each normally contains one set of 23 chromosomes in humans. Haploid describes the chromosome-set number, not the cell's shape. Meiosis distributes inherited chromosome material into different combinations, so equal chromosome counts do not make the resulting cells genetically identical. The detailed chromosome movements and sources of variation will be examined with meiosis later.

Spermatids then undergo differentiation: they become specialised in structure and function. They develop features such as a compact head and a flagellum. Differentiation is a change of form, not a third meiotic division, and it does not halve the chromosome set again. A group of four spermatids can therefore become four sperm without first producing eight cells.

The sequence to follow is primary spermatocyte, two secondary spermatocytes, four haploid spermatids, then specialised sperm. The teacher slide's phrase 'two cycles of meiosis' should be read as two divisions within one meiosis. Spermatogonia, Sertoli cells and interstitial cells are not alternative names for the four final products.

sections.title: A sperm's parts have different jobs
paragraphs: Look at the sperm figure from its head toward its tail. The head contains a nucleus carrying the haploid chromosome set. The acrosome is the cap at the front of the head. Its enzymes help the sperm pass through the egg's surrounding layers. An enzyme is a molecule that speeds a chemical reaction; these enzymes act on material around the egg.

The middle section, or middle piece, contains many mitochondria. These cell structures help supply ATP, a usable chemical energy source for cell activity. The long flagellum is the tail that produces movement. Its movement requires energy. Supplying energy and producing the movement are connected jobs, but they belong to different structures.

Use the label endpoints in the figure to distinguish the small acrosome cap from the whole head, and the short middle section from the long tail. The illustrated sperm is enlarged and simplified so its parts can be compared. Its drawn length does not give an actual travel distance or speed, and its shape alone cannot establish that each part is functioning normally.

Sperm leaving the seminiferous tubules continue to mature in the epididymis, the coiled duct beside the testis. There they acquire the capacity for movement. Further changes occur in the female reproductive tract before fertilization. These later steps do not change where the cells were originally produced or make the epididymis a site of meiosis.

sections.title: Explain the first affected job
paragraphs: A change in a Sertoli cell first concerns the support given to developing sperm. A change in an interstitial cell concerns testosterone release. A change in an acrosome concerns interaction with the egg's surrounding layers. A change in a flagellum concerns movement. Identify the changed part and explain its normal job before predicting the consequence.

Different changes can lead to a similar observation. Poor movement could involve the movement structure or its energy supply. That observation alone does not identify which component failed. Likewise, a normal count of cells does not prove that the acrosomes or tails function normally. Structure, cell number and function provide different pieces of evidence.

We can now connect the whole process. Germ cells develop through division and differentiation, Sertoli cells support them within the tubules, and interstitial cells supply a hormone from between the tubules. The next question is how signals from the brain and pituitary coordinate those cell roles.

worked.title: A movement problem with a different starting point
worked.scenario: A stated classroom model contains sperm with normal-looking heads, acrosomes and tails. The only changed condition is that their mitochondria supply much less ATP than usual. Predict a likely functional effect, and decide whether the appearance of the tails settles the question.
steps: Locate the changed component: mitochondria in the middle piece. Their relevant job is to help supply ATP, rather than carry the main nuclear chromosome set or provide acrosomal enzymes.
Connect the component to the dependent process. Flagellar movement uses energy. Reduced ATP supply can therefore reduce effective movement even when the tail still looks structurally normal.

Test the claim against the given evidence. A photograph can show that a tail is present. It does not measure ATP supply or prove normal movement, so appearance cannot rule out the stated functional problem.

Keep the conclusion within the model. We have not changed the cell count, measured chromosome number or tested acrosomal enzymes. Poor movement alone would not justify claims that meiosis produced no cells or that testosterone release stopped.

optional.question: A model reports many developing reproductive cells inside seminiferous tubules, but the supporting Sertoli cells no longer provide their usual nourishment. Interstitial cells still release testosterone normally. Which job is directly disrupted, and why does the normal hormone result not establish normal sperm development?
optional.answer: The directly disrupted job is local Sertoli-cell support within the tubules. Normal testosterone release from cells between the tubules establishes a different functioning contribution. Developing sperm need the supporting environment as well, so that hormone result alone does not show that development continues normally. The model does not provide enough information to count surviving sperm or diagnose a person.

sections.title: Two pituitary signals reach different cells
paragraphs: Sertoli cells support developing sperm, while interstitial cells release testosterone. Both contribute to reproduction, but a coordinating signal must reach the right target to affect the right job. We will trace each hormone from its release site to its target instead of treating the testis as one undivided target.

The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone, or GnRH. GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary, the hormone-releasing front part of the pituitary gland below the brain. It stimulates release of follicle-stimulating hormone, FSH, and luteinizing hormone, LH. The names refer to functions in the female system, but both hormones also have important male-system targets.

FSH travels in the blood and acts on Sertoli cells within the seminiferous tubules. It supports the Sertoli-cell functions that help sperm develop. LH travels in the blood to interstitial, or Leydig, cells between the tubules and stimulates testosterone release. FSH does not turn a Sertoli cell into a sperm, and LH does not make an interstitial cell become one.

Read the diagram downward from the hypothalamus through GnRH to the anterior pituitary. At the split, follow the left FSH branch to Sertoli cells, then the right LH branch to interstitial cells and testosterone. The green connections represent release or stimulation in this simplified pathway, not ducts carrying sperm. The diagram puts sources, hormones and target cells in separate boxes so you can say what each connection means.

When using the optional textbook p493, keep this distinction: its sentence assigning FSH-stimulated sperm production to interstitial cells is incorrect. FSH supports Sertoli-cell activity; LH stimulates interstitial-cell testosterone production. Developing reproductive cells form the sperm. This distinction agrees with the cell locations on p480 and the two target branches in the teacher diagram.

sections.title: Testosterone supports the tubules and other tissues
paragraphs: Testosterone helps maintain sperm production and reproductive tissues. Within the testis, testosterone and FSH-supported Sertoli-cell activity work together to support spermatogenesis. Trace the diagram's connection from testosterone toward the sperm-support box. The two branches contribute to a shared process without having identical direct targets.

Testosterone also reaches other tissues through the blood. At puberty it contributes to changes such as a deeper voice, facial-hair growth and muscle development. Continued hormone activity helps maintain reproductive function after puberty. A signal affects tissues able to respond to it; its presence in blood does not mean every cell makes the same response.

Androgens are a group of hormones associated with male reproductive development and function. Testosterone is the main androgen followed here. Hormones often associated with one reproductive system can also occur in the other. The effects depend on the signal, its concentration and timing, and the responding tissue.

The phrase 'LH causes facial-hair growth' skips a consequential step. LH first stimulates interstitial cells to release testosterone; testosterone then affects responsive tissues. Distinguishing a direct target from a later effect helps you interpret a diagram or a question that asks what a hormone does directly.

sections.title: Follow the return signal to understand negative feedback
paragraphs: Suppose testosterone rises in a functioning control system. Testosterone-related feedback reduces stimulation from the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. Less GnRH and especially less LH stimulation tends to limit further testosterone production. The response opposes the original rise, which is why it is called negative feedback.

On the diagram, start at the testosterone box and follow the red return line at the right up to the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. The barred endings and minus sign mean inhibition, or reduced stimulation. They do not mean that testosterone flows backward through the green pathway or becomes LH. The dashed return line is a relationship between hormone level and control activity, not a measured time graph.

Now reverse the initial change. If testosterone falls and the control centres still respond normally, its inhibitory feedback is reduced. More GnRH/LH stimulation may then help raise testicular testosterone production. That compensation depends on functioning targets; an increased signal cannot guarantee recovery if the target cells cannot respond.

Sertoli cells also release inhibin. This hormone feeds back to the anterior pituitary to reduce FSH release. Inhibin provides information about the sperm-support pathway, whereas the testosterone loop is especially important for LH control. The retained diagram shows the testosterone loop but does not draw the separate inhibin loop. To describe that omitted loop in words, start at Sertoli cells, name inhibin, then follow it to reduced FSH release from the anterior pituitary.

Negative describes the opposing relationship, not a harmful hormone or a situation in which every quantity falls. A lower starting hormone can lead to stronger upstream stimulation; a higher starting hormone can lead to weaker stimulation. In each case, compare the response with the change that started the loop.

sections.title: An outside androgen can change the control signals
paragraphs: Consider a model in which an outside androgen contributes to the signal detected by the control centres. The increased androgen feedback can suppress GnRH and the pituitary signals FSH and LH. Reduced LH means less stimulation for the testis's own testosterone production; reduced FSH means less Sertoli-cell support. Sperm production can decline despite the added androgen signal.

The distinction is between the hormone signal detected in circulation and the local stimulation needed to maintain testicular activity. An outside source does not reproduce every feature of normal local production. A higher circulating androgen reading is therefore not evidence that more sperm must be produced.

Use 'outside androgen' for this model rather than grouping every performance-related substance together. The teacher slide mentions hGH alongside steroids, but human growth hormone is a protein hormone, not an anabolic steroid. The androgen-feedback explanation here does not establish the effect of every substance or provide directions for hormone use.

If you try the optional numbered hormone diagram, identify what each arrow connects before assigning a name. A hypothalamus-to-pituitary signal, a pituitary-to-interstitial signal, a pituitary-to-Sertoli signal and a returning inhibin signal have different sources and targets. Then read the requested hormone order beneath the image; the order of blanks need not match the order of the diagram numbers. The numbered image compresses the target cells into one testis. Compare it with the labelled Figure 14.13 in the optional textbook on p494 to identify the branches; the drawing alone does not name their cell targets.

These examples explain regulation under stated conditions. They do not diagnose a person's hormone state from appearance or one measurement. We have followed how two cell targets support the male pathway; the female reproductive structures provide the setting for the next set of hormone effects.

worked.title: More signal cannot repair an unresponsive target by itself
worked.scenario: In a hypothetical model, interstitial cells stop responding normally to LH. Testosterone falls, but the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary still detect feedback and can change their output. Predict the direction of upstream stimulation, then decide whether it guarantees restoration of testosterone.
steps: Identify the first changed link: LH can no longer produce its usual response in interstitial cells. The model specifies low testosterone rather than a blocked sperm-transport duct.
Follow the return loop. Lower testosterone reduces inhibitory feedback to the functioning control centres. GnRH/LH stimulation can therefore rise rather than fall.
Follow the forward pathway again. The increased LH still meets the unresponsive target. More signal does not, by itself, restore the missing target response.

Give both parts of the conclusion: upstream stimulation can increase while testosterone remains low. A feedback system attempts to oppose the change, but successful compensation requires its affected parts to work.

Check the limit. The model does not specify every FSH or inhibin change, a measured sperm count, or a treatment. Keep those quantities unresolved instead of extending the LH prediction to every hormone.

optional.question: In a different model, inhibin falls while testosterone stays at its usual level and the anterior pituitary can respond. Which pituitary signal is directly released from inhibin's restraint? Explain why this observation does not by itself require LH to rise.
optional.answer: FSH is directly released from inhibin's inhibitory effect and would tend to rise. The stated change concerns the Sertoli-cell/inhibin feedback loop. Testosterone feedback remains usual in this model, so the observation does not itself establish a corresponding LH rise. Distinguish the two return signals instead of predicting that every pituitary hormone changes together.
